text: Nearly every unmanageable enterprise network started as a reasonable design for a small number of teams. This lesson is about why a design that works fine for three teams can quietly stop working at thirty, and the concrete principles that keep it from happening in the first place.

Three teams peering directly to each other and a shared hub is fine — nine connections, easy to review. The same organization at thirty teams, still peering directly, has roughly four hundred thirty-five potential connections, overlapping IP ranges nobody tracked centrally, and no single place to answer whether team fourteen should even be able to reach team twenty-two. None of the earlier decisions were wrong for the size at the time — the design just never had a built-in answer for growth.

The single most common root cause of an expensive, unplanned redesign is IP address overlap — two spokes independently assigned the same block, discovered only once they need to connect. The fix is a central address plan, a reserved supernet subdivided and allocated to a spoke before it's provisioned, not after, whether that's tracked in a real IPAM tool or a disciplined spreadsheet.

The second principle is a standardized spoke template — an IaC module that stands up a new spoke with the correct CIDR from the central plan, hub connectivity, the routing that forces traffic through the firewall, and the DNS link, already applied. A team onboarding gets a spoke that matches every other spoke structurally, with no chance of someone building the pattern slightly differently each time.

Segmentation should default to deny spoke-to-spoke, so adding spoke thirty-one never requires re-auditing spokes one through thirty — each spoke's access stays scoped to what it actually needs. And ownership has to be explicit: the central team owns the hub, the DNS zones, the IP plan, and the spoke template itself, while each team owns what happens inside its own spoke.

That ownership split is the same guardrails-versus-gates tension this course returns to later, applied specifically to the network layer — a few things need one consistent owner, and everything else should be self-service. That closes Chapter 3. Chapter 4 turns to resilience and disaster recovery for the architecture this chapter just built.
